capabilities.target: arbitrary shell commands inside the agent's container
whole workspace filesystem, including .agent/ and CI/workflow files
push branch / open PR to GitHub repositories

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body, labeled 'bug'
Repository file contents read while reproducing and fixing the issue

instructions.note: Agent is authorized to 'fix it end to end' for any issue labeled bug, with no scope limit on which commands or files it may touch.
The only control against destructive or exfiltrating actions is a prompt instruction; there is no structural egress allowlist or credential scoping behind it.
Defense against prompt injection from issues and code relies entirely on a model-level instruction to ignore embedded instructions, with no structural isolation of untrusted content.
The agent is explicitly authorized to modify its own configuration if it judges extra tools are needed, with no human approval gate, enabling self-directed scope expansion.

elements.name: Any GitHub user able to open issues and add the bug label
Branch push / PR open to GitHub
Shared CI runner hosting the agent's container

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: Enforcement depends entirely on the model choosing to comply; a more capable model can rationalize borderline actions (e.g. framing a secret upload as a diagnostic step) or split exfiltration into steps that individually look benign.

controls.name: Prompt instruction: ignore instructions inside issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: This is an instruction to the same model being targeted by injected content; longer or multi-document injected payloads degrade compliance as the model's reasoning becomes more persuadable by in-context argument.

controls.name: Containerized execution on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: The container isolates the local OS, but outbound network is unrestricted and the mounted credential is a broad org-wide PAT, so the sinks that matter (exfiltration, cross-repo push) remain fully reachable; it does not constrain them.

controls.name: Per-repo, least-privilege credential instead of org-wide PAT
Human approval gate on push, self-config, and unreviewed shell execution
Immutable, externally-enforced agent configuration (no self-edit of .agent/config.yaml)
Max unattended steps / runtime / spend cap
Tamper-evident, attributable action log for commands, writes, and pushes
Pin, scope, and approval-gate new MCP server additions (e.g. Slack)

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue content drives shell execution that can read the org-wide PAT and exfiltrate it over unrestricted egress

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Config.yaml model field changes from a pinned version to a newer one, or evidence of longer/multi-day tasks without an added rate limit.

evidence.observation: Agent is instructed to pick up any issue labeled 'bug' and run whatever shell commands are needed to reproduce and test it, so attacker-opened issue content directly drives shell execution.
network: unrestricted with tools including shell.run and GITHUB_TOKEN set to an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos, both reachable from inside shell.run.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the triggering content untrusted.

recommendations.action: Implement a network egress allowlist excluding attacker-writable destinations.
Replace the org-wide PAT with a least-privilege, short-lived, per-repo credential not exposed to shell.run.
Log and alert on outbound network calls from the agent container.

findings.title: Self-reconfiguration (TC3): untrusted issue content can cause the agent to edit its own .agent/config.yaml to add tools, with no approval

forecast.watch_signal: Any change to .agent/config.yaml's tools list or autonomy level, or the addition of a new MCP server (e.g. planned Slack), without a corresponding review record.

evidence.observation: 'You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task' authorizes the agent to change its own runtime configuration based on its own judgment, with no approval step.
autonomy: full and max_steps: null mean no structural limit stops an unattended, task-driven self-reconfiguration once started.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml immutable at runtime (e.g. mounted read-only); require a separate reviewed deployment to change it.
Require human approval before any tool-scope or autonomy change.
Remove the prompt instruction permitting self-edit of config.

findings.title: Supply-chain execution: repository content reaches unrestricted shell execution with broad credentials

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Rising median steps/runtime per bug-fix task, or a model/version change.

evidence.observation: 'Run whatever commands you need to reproduce and test' means the agent executes code paths present in repository files as part of normal operation.
shell.run has unrestricted network and access to an org-wide PAT, so repository content that influences what gets executed inherits that broad reach.

recommendations.action: Execute untrusted or newly-added repository code in a sandbox with no credential access before granting broad execution.
Require pinned/verified commit provenance for code the agent treats as safe to run.

findings.title: Persistent backdoor via workspace write and push (TC2/TC3 variant): untrusted issue content can cause the agent to write and push arbitrary workspace files, including CI/workflow definitions

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Model/version upgrade, or increasing task duration without added path-based write restrictions.

evidence.observation: fs.write is scoped to 'the whole workspace, including .agent/', meaning the agent can write to any file in the repository, including CI workflow definitions, not only files related to the reported bug.
The fix-test-push flow has no stated restriction on which files may be modified before a branch is pushed and a PR opened.

recommendations.action: Deny-by-default fs.write access to CI/workflow directories unless the task explicitly requires it.
Require human review/approval before pushing changes that touch CI/workflow configuration.

findings.title: No step, runtime, or spend limit on a fully autonomous agent with broad credentials

forecast.watch_signal: Median task runtime trending upward with no corresponding cap added.

evidence.observation: max_steps: null combined with autonomy: full means there is no declared limit on how many actions the agent can take per task.
The agent runs on a shared CI runner with outbound internet; no per-task compute or spend budget is mentioned.

recommendations.action: Set a hard max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes.
Set a spend/compute budget cap per task with a hard stop.

findings.title: No tamper-evident record attributing commands, writes, or pushes to the triggering issue versus a human

forecast.watch_signal: Incident response or compliance review finds no record distinguishing agent actions from human actions.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, or action-attribution mechanism is described in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, or the runtime notes.
A single org-wide PAT is used for all pushes, so GitHub-side attribution would show the service account, not which issue or run triggered the action.

recommendations.action: Add a tamper-evident audit log binding each push/command/config-change to the triggering issue id and commit hash, stored outside the agent's write access.

findings.title: Planned Slack MCP server would let a self-reconfiguring agent add a new, less-controlled egress and input channel

forecast.watch_signal: A Slack MCP server entry appears in MCP client config or a tools/list response.

evidence.observation: 'The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter' is a planned change with no auth, scoping, or pinning details yet specified.
The existing self-config permission ('adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools') is the mechanism by which the agent could itself add or start using a newly available Slack MCP server.

recommendations.action: When added, pin and verify the Slack MCP server's tool definitions, scope its credential narrowly, and require approval before the agent can add it to its own tool list.

stride_coverage.rationale: No other agent or service impersonates issue-fixer; this is a single-agent design with no peer verifying its identity.
The runner's identity is managed by the CI platform; the agent does not authenticate peer runners in this design.
Artifacts do not describe whether other tenants on the shared runner can write into this agent's container or vice versa.
The runner performs no actions attributable to a principal; repudiation is assessed at the agent process, not shared infrastructure.
Runtime notes state the runner is 'shared' with outbound internet but do not describe tenant isolation mechanisms.
No information on resource quotas or scheduling fairness on the shared runner is given.
No information on whether a container escape on this shared runner would grant access to other tenants' credentials.
GitHub's own account system provides login-bound attribution for issue authors; that is GitHub's platform concern, not this agent's design.
GitHub.com's identity as the remote host is fixed infrastructure authenticated via TLS/API; spoofing GitHub itself is outside this design's threat model.
Slack MCP server is only planned for next quarter; no authentication or identity-verification design has been specified yet.
Same reason: the planned Slack integration has no design details yet on attribution of its actions.
Artifacts do not state whether the repository itself holds confidential data beyond what the bug-fix task needs.
A file store does not itself enforce rate or availability limits; the relevant denial-of-service risk is scored on the agent process.
config.yaml references ${ORG_WIDE_PAT} as an environment variable, not a literal secret in the file; whether the resolved value is readable via this store isn't fully specified.
Configuration store availability does not bound agent execution; the relevant denial-of-service risk is scored on the agent process.
This is an inbound flow carrying issue content into the agent; it does not carry the agent's data outward.
This outbound network flow carries data out, not configuration or code into the agent; inbound tampering is scored on the issue input flow.
Artifacts do not indicate whether commit contents are scanned for secrets before push.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted GitHub issue (any user can open one and add the 'bug' label) drives a fully autonomous agent (A4, no step limit) that holds an org-wide, repo+workflow-scoped PAT to execute arbitrary shell commands, write anywhere in the workspace including its own config, and push to GitHub, with no human approval gate at any step (find.lethal_trifecta_shell, find.self_reconfig, find.persistent_backdoor each reach an S2/S3 sink from a U source and hit the autonomy modifier). The only present controls are two behavioral prompt instructions (never delete/exfiltrate; ignore embedded instructions) and a container that does not constrain the sink (unrestricted egress, broad credential still reachable), which together earn exactly one tier of step-4 credit per finding, holding residual at high. Two property gaps compound this: no step/runtime/spend limit (find.no_step_limit) and no attributable audit trail separating agent actions from human ones (find.no_audit_trail), both capped at high per rubric 5a. Forecast returns to critical: a model upgrade or longer task horizons defeat the dependent prompt instructions currently holding residual down, and the planned Slack MCP server (find.slack_mcp_forecast) would add a new, as-yet-unscoped egress and input channel reachable through the agent's existing self-configuration permission. The single highest-leverage fix is replacing the org-wide broad-scope PAT with a least-privilege, per-repo credential with no shell/env access, combined with making .agent/config.yaml immutable at runtime.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes provided; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior, logs, or a live red-team test of the deployed agent.
No MCP server manifest, tool schema, or IaC was provided for github.push_branch/github.open_pr; their exact scoping and validation is inferred from config.yaml and the id table.

The trust level of repository file contents (in.repo_files) is inferred as internal; no branch-protection or code-review policy was provided, so this could be optimistic if the repo accepts unreviewed external contributions.
No information was provided on logging, monitoring, or audit tooling actually deployed; absence of evidence for an audit trail is treated as absence of the control (find.no_audit_trail).

The planned Slack MCP server is assessed only as a forecast (find.slack_mcp_forecast) because no design details exist yet; this assessment should be rerun once that integration is designed (trigger: new_mcp_server).
